Let’s dive into Chapter 6—Navigating Obstacles to Self-Compassion.
Even when you understand just how important self-compassion is, it’s pretty common to hit some internal roadblocks along the way. Maybe you’ve noticed old beliefs or emotional habits popping up, making the practice feel awkward or even impossible at times. Recognizing these barriers—and facing them with a gentle attitude—is an essential part of weaving self-compassion into your everyday life.
One of the biggest hurdles? That nagging fear that being kind to yourself will somehow make you lazy or complacent. Have you ever worried that softening up means you’ll lose your edge, or stop pushing yourself to grow? Here’s the thing: self-compassion doesn’t kill motivation—it actually fuels it. When you stop being so afraid of messing up, you create a safe space to try new things and learn from your mistakes. People who feel cared for are often more willing to take healthy risks and keep moving forward.
Another common belief is that self-criticism is the only way to hold yourself accountable. Maybe you’ve grown up thinking you have to be tough on yourself to stay on track. But research—and real life—show us something different. Think about an athlete who has a bad game. If they respond with curiosity and understanding instead of harshness, they’re much more likely to learn and improve. Gentle honesty works better than beating yourself up.
Shame and feelings of unworthiness can also stand in the way. If you’ve faced criticism or rejection in the past, you might feel like you don’t deserve kindness—even from yourself. This can turn into a cycle where self-judgment just deepens those feelings of not being enough. Breaking that cycle takes time, patience, and a willingness to challenge those old stories you’ve been telling yourself.
So, how do you actually move through these obstacles? Here are a few gentle strategies to try:
First, just notice resistance when it comes up. If self-compassion feels uncomfortable, pause for a moment and acknowledge it—without judging yourself for how you feel.
Next, get curious about what’s underneath. Where does that fear or resistance come from? Is it really helping you, or is it just an old habit?
Start small. Pick minor situations and practice being kind to yourself there. As you get more comfortable, you’ll build confidence and trust in the process.
And don’t be afraid to reach out for support. Talking things over with a trusted friend or a professional can make you realize you’re not alone—and that encouragement can mean a lot.
Over time, these gentle steps can help soften your resistance, making self-compassion feel more and more natural. Think of it like learning a new language: it takes practice and patience, but the rewards are absolutely worth it.
